one_liner: C++20 streaming SAX-style XML push parser with zero-copy callbacks; author-measured 4.4x faster than libxml2's SAX2 streaming parser.
what_it_does: Parses XML incrementally from chunks you push (feedInput) or from a std::istream (readStream). It calls the virtual openTag/closeTag/rawTextData methods on your XmlParserInterface subclass, never builds a tree, and uses constant memory. Attribute values arrive entity-decoded. Text arrives raw and may be split across several calls; you decode it with the supplied decodeXmlChars. An optional SpeedyXmlDispatcher layer compiles a declarative element schema into member-function callbacks, skips subtrees the schema does not describe, and can collect and decode text per node. The API is unrelated to libxml2's SAX2, xmlReader and DOM APIs.
how_it_is_fast: Nearly all scanning goes through memchr: '<' ends a text run, then '>' ends the tag, then '=', the quote character and '&' are found inside attributes. Tag-name ends are found with an 8-bytes-per-step SWAR bit trick instead of SIMD intrinsics. Callbacks get std::string_view slices of the caller's buffer, so the parser copies only tags that straddle a slice boundary. It also skips work a conforming parser does: no text entity decoding, no namespace or DTD processing, no encoding handling, and no start/end-tag matching unless the optional validation layer is on. Predefined entities in attributes are matched with 32-bit word compares, and setEnableTextEvent(false), which the dispatcher toggles automatically, turns off text callbacks for elements you ignore.
when_to_use: Single-pass extraction from very large or unbounded UTF-8 XML dumps (Wikipedia, OpenStreetMap, StackExchange, dblp-style exports) that are too big to hold as a DOM
Single-core ETL where libxml2 SAX2 or Expat is the bottleneck: the author's 8-dataset chart shows libxml2 at 6-29% and Expat at 2-11% of SpeedyXml's throughput
Input arriving in arbitrary chunks from sockets or files: feedInput accepts any slice boundary (tests feed 1-byte slices, the fuzz harness 1-97 bytes), and ~1 MiB slices are recommended for speed
Documents with a known schema where you want callbacks only on specific paths: the Dispatcher skips unlisted subtrees by depth counting and switches text events off outside collectText/onText nodes
Codebases that want a BSD-3-Clause, dependency-free parser they can vendor as one header plus one .cpp
when_not_to_use: You need a tree, XPath or random access: it is push-only, so a DOM parser (pugixml, RapidXml, libsimdxml) fits better
UTF-16 or Latin-1 input, documents with an internal DTD subset or custom entities (rejected), or anything needing namespace resolution: none of these are supported, and libxml2 handles them
Untrusted input that must be well-formed: it is not a validating parser, and without enableValidation_TagNesting it accepts mismatched and unclosed tags

Big-endian targets (a static_assert rejects them), or teams that need a proven dependency: it went public 2026-07-27 with one release (v1.0.0), has 1 star and no third-party users, and CI runs only on Ubuntu with GCC and Clang

Workloads that need decoded text for every node: the published timings use no-op callbacks that never decode text, so the cost of calling decodeXmlChars or collectText yourself is not included in them

integration.form: static lib (CMake target SpeedyXml) or source-drop of include/SpeedyXml/SpeedyXml.h + src/SpeedyXml.cpp (add SpeedyXmlDispatcher.h/.cpp for the schema layer)
integration.dependencies: none (C++ standard library only); expat, pugixml, libxml2 and RapidXml are used only by the optional bench tool
integration.min_toolchain: C++20 (uses std::span and <bit>); CMake 3.20 for the CMake build; minimum GCC/Clang versions not documented (CI uses the current Ubuntu GCC and Clang)
integration.platforms: any little-endian target (enforced by static_assert); no SIMD intrinsics (portable SWAR + memchr); CI runs only on GitHub ubuntu-latest, and macOS, Windows and MSVC are untested
integration.thread_safety: not documented for XmlStreamParser, and each instance holds mutable buffers, so use one per stream/thread; the dispatcher docs say a compiled XmlSchema is immutable and can drive any number of parsers concurrently

gotchas: Every string_view (tag name, attribute, text) is valid only inside the callback, so copy what you keep. rawTextData can fire several times per text node, including whitespace-only pieces, and unlike attributes its text is not entity-decoded.

isValidEndOfDocument() checks only the parser state and trailing text, so `` or an unclosed root passes unless you call enableValidation_TagNesting(). That layer reports errors by throwing XmlValidationException (default maxDepth 64), while syntax errors are reported by feedInput returning false plus getError().

The encoding declaration is ignored, so non-UTF-8 bytes are passed through, not rejected. Per the source, a leading UTF-8 BOM reaches you as a text event. Unknown named entities such as ä (declared in external DTDs) stay undecoded, and processing instructions are skipped silently.

feedInput takes an int length, so slices must be under 2 GiB. readStream reads through a fixed 64 KiB stack buffer, but the README says ~1 MiB slices give the best performance (the bench uses 1 MiB), so on hot paths call feedInput with your own large buffer. Tags that straddle slices are buffered up to setMaxBufferSize (default 1 MiB), then the parse fails.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: RapidXml, libsimdxml and Parshred's headline numbers are for DOM/index parsers that need the whole document in memory. Pick SpeedyXml for constant-memory, single-pass streaming of multi-hundred-MiB or unbounded input, with a BSD-3-Clause license and no ISA requirements; pick Parshred (AGPL-3.0, with SAX/pull/streaming APIs, namespaces, DTD validation and XPath) or libsimdxml (XPath) when you need standards coverage or queries.
verified_claims_summary: The author's own bench tool times each parser once, by wall clock, on a 235 MiB document that is neither named nor published: SpeedyXml 0.34 s vs 1.53 s (4.4x) for libxml2's SAX2 push parser, both fed 1 MiB chunks with no-op element callbacks, plus pugixml DOM 1.00 s, RapidXml 1.29 s and Expat 4.38 s. An 8-dataset chart puts libxml2 at 6-29% of SpeedyXml's throughput (about 3.4x slower on treebank, up to 17x on text-heavy Wikipedia). Compiler, flags, CPU and libxml2 version are not stated. The timings include file reads, SpeedyXml always runs last, and it does less work than libxml2 (no text decoding, namespaces, DTDs or tag matching).
status_note: Active but brand-new: the code history goes back to Feb 2025, it went public 2026-07-27 as v1.0.0, and the last commit is 2026-07-29. It is BSD-3-Clause and dependency-free, easy to vendor (two core files), fuzzed with libFuzzer and tested in CI under ASan/UBSan.
